title: fdid – User Manual
text:
Welcome
This book is the public tutorial for the fdid R package, which implements Factorial Difference-in-Differences (FDID) for panel data settings where all units experience a common event and differ in a baseline factor G (Xu, Zhao, and Ding 2026).
The tutorial is organized around the target the analyst wants to report. The binary and discrete-G workflow comes first. Continuous-G workflows then separate scalar slopes, level curves, derivative curves, observed-population average derivatives, fixed-reference contrasts, and support diagnostics.
Main user-facing functions:

title: fdid – User Manual
text:
Organization

Chapter 1  Get Started covers installation, loading, and the required data shape.
Chapter 2  Binary G covers the original binary/discrete-G workflow.
Chapter 3  Continuous-G Overview maps user targets to continuous-G methods, support checks, and reporting views.
Chapter 4  Kernel Estimator for Continuous G covers kernel level and derivative curves.
Chapter 5  DML Estimators for Continuous G covers DML scalar, flexible-curve, and incremental targets.
Chapter 6  Visualization Options documents current base-graphics plotting.
Chapter 7  Reporting And Inference centralizes summaries, contrasts, derivatives, and interval labels.
Chapter 8  Sensitivity Analysis gives applied sensitivity checks.

Report bugs
Please report bugs on GitHub with minimal replicable code, data, and a treatment-status plot when relevant.






Cao, Jiarui, Yiqing Xu, and Chuanchuan Zhang. 2022. “Clans and Calamity: How Social Capital Saved Lives During China’s Great Famine.” Journal of Development Economics 157: 102865.


Cinelli, Carlos, and Chad Hazlett. 2020. “Making Sense of Sensitivity: Extending Omitted Variable Bias.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B 82 (1): 39–67.

title: 1  Get Started
text:
1.1 Installation
This chapter covers only the setup needed to run the tutorial: install or load fdid, load the example data, and prepare the wide panel shape used by fdid().
Install the package from GitHub for ordinary use:
install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("xuyiqing/fdid")
When reviewing a local source checkout, install the local source into the R library that will be used for rendering:
R CMD build fdid
R CMD INSTALL fdid_<version>.tar.gz
After installation, restart R and confirm the package path:
library(fdid)
packageVersion("fdid")
normalizePath(find.package("fdid"))

title: 1  Get Started
text:
1.2 Dataset
The tutorial uses the package’s famine mortality data. The raw data are long panel data: each unit has multiple year rows, an outcome, a baseline factor G, and covariates. fdid_prepare() converts this layout to one row per unit with one outcome column per time period.

library(fdid)
data(fdid)

mortality$uniqueid <- paste(
  mortality$provid,
  mortality$countyid,
  sep = "-"
)

covar <- c("avggrain", "nograin", "urban", "dis_bj", "dis_pc",
           "rice", "minority", "edu", "lnpop")

s <- fdid_prepare(
  data = mortality,
  Y_label = "mortality",
  X_labels = covar,
  G_label = "pczupu",
  unit_label = "uniqueid",
  time_label = "year"
)

str(s)

The prepared object is the input to fdid(). It contains G, covariates, and wide outcome columns such as Y_1957, Y_1958, and later years. The following chapters reuse this pattern for binary, discrete, and continuous baseline factors.






Cao, Jiarui, Yiqing Xu, and Chuanchuan Zhang. 2022. “Clans and Calamity: How Social Capital Saved Lives During China’s Great Famine.” Journal of Development Economics 157: 102865.


Cinelli, Carlos, and Chad Hazlett. 2020. “Making Sense of Sensitivity: Extending Omitted Variable Bias.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B 82 (1): 39–67.


Xu, Yiqing, Anqi Zhao, and Peng Ding. 2026. “Factorial Difference-in-Differences.” Journal of the American Statistical Association, no. just-accepted: 1–23.

title: 2  Binary G
text:
2.1 Data preparation
This chapter shows the original binary/discrete-G FDID workflow. Use this path when the estimand is a treated-versus-control contrast or a comparison between a small number of baseline-factor groups.
fdid_prepare() expects long panel data and returns the wide object consumed by fdid().
library(fdid)
data(fdid)

mortality$uniqueid <- paste(mortality$provid, mortality$countyid, sep = "-")
mortality$highzupu <- ifelse(
  mortality$pczupu >= median(mortality$pczupu, na.rm = TRUE),
  1,
  0
)

covar <- c("avggrain", "nograin", "urban", "dis_bj", "dis_pc",
           "rice", "minority", "edu", "lnpop")

s_binary <- fdid_prepare(
  data = mortality,
  Y_label = "mortality",
  X_labels = covar,
  G_label = "highzupu",
  unit_label = "uniqueid",
  time_label = "year"
)
If cluster-robust inference is needed, pass cluster_label to fdid_prepare() so the prepared object carries the clustering variable through estimation.

title: 2  Binary G
text:
2.2 FDID: A quick review
FDID compares how outcomes change around a common event across units with different baseline factor values. For the famine example, the event period is 1958-1961 and the reference year is 1957.

tr_period <- 1958:1961
ref_period <- 1957

title: 2  Binary G
text:
2.3 Estimation
The binary/discrete workflow uses the traditional methods exposed through the same fdid() interface.

2.3.1 Difference-in-Differences

fit_did <- fdid(
  s_binary,
  tr_period = tr_period,
  ref_period = ref_period,
  method = "did",
  vartype = "robust"
)
summary(fit_did)


2.3.2 OLS without interactions

fit_ols1 <- fdid(
  s_binary,
  tr_period = tr_period,
  ref_period = ref_period,
  method = "ols1",
  vartype = "robust"
)
summary(fit_ols1)


2.3.3 OLS with interactions

fit_ols2 <- fdid(
  s_binary,
  tr_period = tr_period,
  ref_period = ref_period,
  method = "ols2",
  vartype = "robust"
)
summary(fit_ols2)


2.3.4 Entropy balancing

fit_ebal <- fdid(
  s_binary,
  tr_period = tr_period,
  ref_period = ref_period,
  method = "ebal",
  target.pop = "1",
  vartype = "robust"
)
summary(fit_ebal)


2.3.5 IPW

fit_ipw <- fdid(
  s_binary,
  tr_period = tr_period,
  ref_period = ref_period,
  method = "ipw",
  vartype = "robust"
)
summary(fit_ipw)


2.3.6 AIPW

fit_aipw <- fdid(
  s_binary,
  tr_period = tr_period,
  ref_period = ref_period,
  method = "aipw",
  vartype = "robust"
)
summary(fit_aipw)

title: 2  Binary G
text:
2.4 Inference
Binary/discrete methods support robust, bootstrap, and jackknife variance choices where available. Use robust inference for fast first checks and bootstrap or jackknife when the design calls for a resampling comparison.

fit_ols1_boot <- fdid(
  s_binary,
  tr_period = tr_period,
  ref_period = ref_period,
  method = "ols1",
  vartype = "bootstrap",
  nsims = 199,
  parallel = FALSE
)

title: 2  Binary G
text:
2.5 Estimation options
target.pop controls whether weighted estimators target the G = 1, G = 0, or combined population where the method supports that choice. entire_period controls whether all periods or a shorter event window enter the dynamic output. missing_data controls how incomplete rows are handled.

title: 2  Binary G
text:
2.6 Plotting the results

2.6.1 Raw means by group

plot(fit_ols1, type = "raw", connected = TRUE)


2.6.2 Dynamic estimates

plot(fit_ols1, type = "dynamic", connected = TRUE)


2.6.3 Diagnostic test for overlap

plot(fit_aipw, type = "overlap")


2.6.4 Comparison of methods

fits <- fdid_list(fit_did, fit_ols1, fit_ols2, fit_ebal, fit_ipw, fit_aipw)
plot(fits)

The continuous-G chapters start from a different question. Once G is continuous, a scalar slope, level curve, derivative curve, average derivative, and fixed-reference contrast are different targets. Choose the target first, then choose the method.






Cao, Jiarui, Yiqing Xu, and Chuanchuan Zhang. 2022. “Clans and Calamity: How Social Capital Saved Lives During China’s Great Famine.” Journal of Development Economics 157: 102865.


Cinelli, Carlos, and Chad Hazlett. 2020. “Making Sense of Sensitivity: Extending Omitted Variable Bias.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B 82 (1): 39–67.


Xu, Yiqing, Anqi Zhao, and Peng Ding. 2026. “Factorial Difference-in-Differences.” Journal of the American Statistical Association, no. just-accepted: 1–23.

title: 3  Continuous-G Overview
text:
3.1 Choose the Target First
This chapter is the target map for continuous-G analysis. It does not try to fit every estimator. It explains which object you want, how to prepare the design, why support comes before estimation, and which chapter gives the full workflow.
Continuous-G methods do not estimate one interchangeable object. Decide whether the report needs a scalar, a curve, a derivative, a contrast, or a diagnostic display before choosing method.
Keep four concepts separate:

title: 3  Continuous-G Overview
text:
3.2 Prepare the Continuous-G Design
Use a continuous baseline factor in fdid_prepare(). The example below uses lnpczupu, a log social-capital measure from the mortality data.

library(fdid)
data(fdid)

mortality$uniqueid <- paste(mortality$provid, mortality$countyid, sep = "-")

covar <- c("avggrain", "nograin", "urban", "dis_bj", "dis_pc",
           "rice", "minority", "edu", "lnpop")

s_cont <- fdid_prepare(
  data = transform(mortality, G_cont = lnpczupu),
  Y_label = "mortality",
  X_labels = covar,
  G_label = "G_cont",
  unit_label = "uniqueid",
  time_label = "year"
)

tr_period <- 1958:1961
ref_period <- 1957

For curve methods, eval_g is an estimation grid. The package estimates and stores curve quantities at those values; plotting displays the stored grid rather than densifying the curve after the fact.

g_positive <- s_cont$G[s_cont$G > 0]
eval_g <- as.numeric(stats::quantile(
  g_positive,
  probs = seq(0.20, 0.80, length.out = 9),
  na.rm = TRUE
))

title: 3  Continuous-G Overview
text:
3.3 Inspect Support Before Estimation
Continuous-G curve estimates are weakest where observed support is sparse. Inspect the empirical distribution of G before fitting a curve and avoid turning a tail extrapolation into a headline result.

hist(s_cont$G, breaks = 35, col = "gray85", border = "white",
     xlab = "Baseline factor G", main = "Observed support")
abline(v = range(eval_g), col = c("steelblue", "firebrick"), lwd = 2)
rug(s_cont$G, col = grDevices::adjustcolor("black", 0.25))

text:

“The scalar summary is the main result”

“It is just the average plotted slope”

“All contrast intervals use the same variance source”

“The support display is adjusted causal evidence”

title: 3  Continuous-G Overview
text:
3.5 What Not To Compare Directly
Do not line up dml_plr, kernel, dml_flex, and dml_incremental as if they estimate the same number. dml_plr is a scalar partially linear slope. kernel and dml_flex can report level and derivative curves. dml_incremental is an observed-population average derivative, not the average of a plotted dml_flex derivative curve. A fixed-reference contrast is a function of a stored level curve, not a new estimator.






Cao, Jiarui, Yiqing Xu, and Chuanchuan Zhang. 2022. “Clans and Calamity: How Social Capital Saved Lives During China’s Great Famine.” Journal of Development Economics 157: 102865.


Cinelli, Carlos, and Chad Hazlett. 2020. “Making Sense of Sensitivity: Extending Omitted Variable Bias.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B 82 (1): 39–67.


Xu, Yiqing, Anqi Zhao, and Peng Ding. 2026. “Factorial Difference-in-Differences.” Journal of the American Statistical Association, no. just-accepted: 1–23.

title: 4  Kernel Estimator for Continuous G
text:
4.1 When Kernel Is The Right First Curve
The kernel estimator is the transparent first curve workflow for continuous G. It estimates a level curve mu(g) and a derivative curve delta(g) over the supplied eval_g grid.
Use method = "kernel" when the main object is a smooth curve and you want a direct view of how the FDID response changes with G. It is especially useful as a first curve because the evaluation grid, bandwidth, and support choices are explicit.
crumbs: 4  Kernel Estimator for Continuous G

title: 4  Kernel Estimator for Continuous G
text:
4.2 Evaluation Grid And Bandwidth

fit_kernel <- fdid(
  s_cont,
  tr_period = tr_period,
  ref_period = ref_period,
  method = "kernel",
  eval_g = eval_g,
  h0 = 0.18,
  vartype = "robust"
)

eval_g is the grid where level and derivative quantities are estimated. Leaving h0 = NULL requests bandwidth selection; setting h0 fixes the bandwidth for reproducibility or sensitivity checks.
crumbs: 4  Kernel Estimator for Continuous G

title: 4  Kernel Estimator for Continuous G
text:
4.3 Level Curve

plot(fit_kernel, type = "curve", curve = "level",
     interval = "pointwise", Xdistr = "rug")

The level curve is the fitted event-period response mu(g).
crumbs: 4  Kernel Estimator for Continuous G

title: 4  Kernel Estimator for Continuous G
text:
4.4 Derivative Curve

plot(fit_kernel, type = "curve", curve = "derivative",
     interval = "pointwise", Xdistr = "rug")

The derivative curve is the local slope delta(g) on the evaluation grid. Derivative interpretation is more sensitive to bandwidth and support than level interpretation.
crumbs: 4  Kernel Estimator for Continuous G

title: 4  Kernel Estimator for Continuous G
text:
4.5 Pointwise Analytical Intervals
With vartype = "robust", kernel pointwise intervals use stored analytical standard errors for each grid point. They are pointwise intervals, not uniform bands.
crumbs: 4  Kernel Estimator for Continuous G

title: 4  Kernel Estimator for Continuous G
text:
4.6 Bootstrap Pointwise Intervals
With vartype = "bootstrap", kernel pointwise intervals use stored bootstrap curve replicates.

fit_kernel_boot <- fdid(
  s_cont,
  tr_period = tr_period,
  ref_period = ref_period,
  method = "kernel",
  eval_g = eval_g,
  h0 = 0.18,
  vartype = "bootstrap",
  boot = 199,
  parallel = FALSE
)

Use substantially more replications in a final empirical report than in a fast tutorial render.
crumbs: 4  Kernel Estimator for Continuous G

title: 4  Kernel Estimator for Continuous G
text:
4.7 Bootstrap Quantile-Envelope Bands
Kernel bootstrap bands are finite-grid quantile-envelope bands over stored bootstrap curves. They should not be described as studentized sup-t bands.

plot(fit_kernel_boot, type = "curve", curve = "level",
     interval = "both", show.uniform.CI = TRUE)
crumbs: 4  Kernel Estimator for Continuous G

title: 4  Kernel Estimator for Continuous G
text:
4.8 Contrast And Derivative Reporting
Use reporting helpers when the table needs a value, a level contrast, or a fixed-G derivative instead of the whole plot.

fdid_contrast(fit_kernel_boot, g0 = eval_g[2], g1 = eval_g[7])
fdid_derivative(fit_kernel_boot, g0 = eval_g[5])
plot(fit_kernel_boot, type = "contrast", ref.g = "median",
     target.type = "quantile", target.g = 5)

Exact-grid reporting can use stored covariance or replicate information when available. Interpolated reporting should be labeled as interpolated.
crumbs: 4  Kernel Estimator for Continuous G

title: 4  Kernel Estimator for Continuous G
text:
4.9 Kernel Option Checklist

Choose an interior eval_g grid with enough support.
Compare at least one bandwidth sensitivity run.
Label analytical intervals as pointwise.
Label bootstrap bands as quantile-envelope bands.
Report fixed-reference contrasts through fdid_contrast() or plot(type = "contrast").







Cao, Jiarui, Yiqing Xu, and Chuanchuan Zhang. 2022. “Clans and Calamity: How Social Capital Saved Lives During China’s Great Famine.” Journal of Development Economics 157: 102865.


Cinelli, Carlos, and Chad Hazlett. 2020. “Making Sense of Sensitivity: Extending Omitted Variable Bias.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B 82 (1): 39–67.


Xu, Yiqing, Anqi Zhao, and Peng Ding. 2026. “Factorial Difference-in-Differences.” Journal of the American Statistical Association, no. just-accepted: 1–23.

title: 5  DML Estimators for Continuous G
text:
5.1 DML Targets
DML workflows in fdid are target-specific orthogonal-score workflows. Do not treat them as interchangeable estimators for one quantity.
All continuous-treatment DML paths use the FDID first-difference outcome Delta Y_i = mean(Y_i, event) - Y_i, ref conceptually, then apply cross-fitted nuisance learning and target-specific orthogonal scores.
crumbs: 5  DML Estimators for Continuous G

title: 5  DML Estimators for Continuous G
text:
Method
Target
Main output



dml_plr
Scalar partially linear dose slope
summary()


dml_flex
Flexible level curve theta(g) and derivative theta_prime(g)

curve plots, fdid_contrast(), fdid_derivative()



dml_incremental
Observed-population average derivative

summary() and density diagnostics


dml_binary
Binary-G AIPW/IRM contrast
summary()
crumbs: 5  DML Estimators for Continuous G

title: 5  DML Estimators for Continuous G
text:
5.2 dml_plr: Scalar Linear Dose Slope

fit_plr <- fdid(
  s_cont,
  tr_period = tr_period,
  ref_period = ref_period,
  method = "dml_plr",
  learner = "linear",
  K = 3,
  S = 1,
  dml_inference = "score"
)
summary(fit_plr)

dml_plr is a scalar benchmark. It should not be described as the whole continuous-G curve.
crumbs: 5  DML Estimators for Continuous G

title: 5  DML Estimators for Continuous G
section: 5.3 dml_flex: Flexible Level And Derivative Curves
text:
5.3 dml_flex: Flexible Level And Derivative Curves

fit_flex <- fdid(
  s_cont,
  tr_period = tr_period,
  ref_period = ref_period,
  method = "dml_flex",
  learner = "linear",
  eval_g = eval_g,
  K = 3,
  S = 1,
  density_method = "residual_kde",
  signal_map = "spline",
  boot = 199
)

plot(fit_flex, type = "curve", curve = "level")
plot(fit_flex, type = "curve", curve = "derivative")

dml_flex targets a flexible level curve and derivative curve after nuisance adjustment. Derivative estimates are usually more fragile than level estimates.
crumbs: 5  DML Estimators for Continuous G

title: 5  DML Estimators for Continuous G
text:
5.4 dml_incremental: Observed Average Derivative

fit_incremental <- fdid(
  s_cont,
  tr_period = tr_period,
  ref_period = ref_period,
  method = "dml_incremental",
  learner = "linear",
  K = 3,
  S = 1,
  density_method = "residual_kde"
)
summary(fit_incremental)

dml_incremental reports an observed-population average derivative. It is not merely the average of a plotted dml_flex derivative curve.
crumbs: 5  DML Estimators for Continuous G

title: 5  DML Estimators for Continuous G
text:
5.5 Learners, Cross-Fitting, And Repeated Splits
learner controls nuisance models. Linear learners are fast and transparent; lasso, ridge, elasticnet, ranger, grf, gam, nnet, and xgboost are available when their packages are installed. K controls cross-fitting folds and S controls repeated splits. Use small values for exploratory checks and larger values for final robustness when runtime allows.
crumbs: 5  DML Estimators for Continuous G

title: 5  DML Estimators for Continuous G
text:
5.6 Conditional Density Choices
density_method controls the conditional density f_{G|X}(g|x) for dml_flex and dml_incremental.






density_method
Practical role



residual_kde
Fast default; KDE of residualized G



location_scale
Allows heteroskedastic G | X through a scale model


local_kde
More local and more sensitive to covariate dimension



Treat density choice as a sensitivity dimension.
crumbs: 5  DML Estimators for Continuous G

title: 5  DML Estimators for Continuous G
section: 5.7 BLP Spline Is A Signal Map, Not A Density Estimator
text:
5.7 BLP Spline Is A Signal Map, Not A Density Estimator
signal_map controls how the cross-fitted dml_flex signal is mapped to the evaluation grid. signal_map = "blp_spline" is a B-spline best linear projection signal map. It is not a density_method.
crumbs: 5  DML Estimators for Continuous G

title: 5  DML Estimators for Continuous G
text:
5.8 DML Inference Labels

Scalar DML robust intervals come from orthogonal-score variance.
Scalar score-multiplier intervals use multiplier draws over stored influence values.
Non-BLP dml_flex bands are practical signal-mapping multiplier bands.

signal_map = "blp_spline" stores finite-grid covariance matrices and can use Gaussian max-t bands when usable.
crumbs: 5  DML Estimators for Continuous G

title: 5  DML Estimators for Continuous G
text:
5.9 DML Diagnostics
Check signal summaries, density diagnostics, low-density shares, derivative nuisance diagnostics, cluster counts when clustering is used, and repeated split stability. Diagnostics are part of the DML result object and should be reported when they explain a substantive choice.






Cao, Jiarui, Yiqing Xu, and Chuanchuan Zhang. 2022. “Clans and Calamity: How Social Capital Saved Lives During China’s Great Famine.” Journal of Development Economics 157: 102865.


Cinelli, Carlos, and Chad Hazlett. 2020. “Making Sense of Sensitivity: Extending Omitted Variable Bias.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B 82 (1): 39–67.


Xu, Yiqing, Anqi Zhao, and Peng Ding. 2026. “Factorial Difference-in-Differences.” Journal of the American Statistical Association, no. just-accepted: 1–23.
crumbs: 5  DML Estimators for Continuous G

title: 6  Visualization Options
text:
6.1 Raw, Dynamic, And Overlap Displays
This chapter documents the current base-graphics plotting behavior. The package-wide ggplot/autoplot modernization is deferred and should not be promised as current behavior.
plot(fit_ols1, type = "raw", connected = TRUE)
plot(fit_ols1, type = "dynamic", connected = TRUE)
plot(fit_aipw, type = "overlap")
Raw plots show descriptive outcome means. Dynamic plots show time-indexed FDID estimates. Overlap plots are propensity-score diagnostics for binary methods that store propensity scores.

title: 6  Visualization Options
text:
6.2 Continuous-G Curve Displays

plot(fit_kernel, type = "curve", curve = "level")
plot(fit_flex, type = "curve", curve = "level")

For kernel and dml_flex, the curve plot displays stored eval_g rows. It does not re-estimate or densify the curve inside plot().

title: 6  Visualization Options
text:
6.3 Level, Derivative, And Both

plot(fit_kernel, type = "curve", curve = "level")
plot(fit_kernel, type = "curve", curve = "derivative")
plot(fit_kernel, type = "curve", curve = "both")

Use explicit curve values in reports so readers know which target is being shown.

title: 6  Visualization Options
text:
6.4 Pointwise Versus Stored Uniform/Simultaneous Intervals
interval = "pointwise" displays pointwise intervals when available. interval = "uniform" or show.uniform.CI = TRUE uses stored bands when the fit contains them. Kernel bootstrap bands are quantile-envelope bands. Non-BLP dml_flex bands are practical signal-mapping multiplier bands. BLP-spline DML can use finite-grid covariance/Gaussian max-t bands when usable.

title: 6  Visualization Options
section: 6.5 Support Displays: Rug, Density, Histogram, Separate Panel
text:
6.5 Support Displays: Rug, Density, Histogram, Separate Panel

plot(fit_kernel, type = "curve", Xdistr = "rug")
plot(fit_kernel, type = "curve", Xdistr = "density")
plot(fit_kernel, type = "curve", Xdistr = "histogram",
     support.panel = "separate")

Support displays are descriptive overlays or panels. They help identify sparse regions of G; they are not adjusted causal estimates.

title: 6  Visualization Options
text:
6.6 Evaluation-Grid And Marked-G Displays

plot(fit_kernel, type = "curve", show.eval_g = TRUE,
     diff.values = c(eval_g[2], eval_g[5], eval_g[8]))

Use evaluation-grid ticks and marked values to connect plot features with reported contrasts or derivative values.

title: 6  Visualization Options
text:
6.7 Fixed-Reference Contrast Coefficient Plot

plot(fit_kernel, type = "contrast", ref.g = "median",
     target.type = "quantile", target.g = 5)

The contrast plot displays level differences relative to a reference value. It delegates estimates and intervals to fdid_contrast() and includes an algebraic-zero reference row by default.

title: 6  Visualization Options
text:
6.8 Styling And Base-Graphics Arguments
Plots use base graphics and accept ordinary arguments such as main, xlab, ylab, xlim, ylim, colors, line widths, point characters, and support display controls. Save and restore par() if you change multi-panel layout in your own scripts.

title: 6  Visualization Options
section: 6.9 What Will Change If The Package-Wide Plotting Layer Is Implemented
text:
6.9 What Will Change If The Package-Wide Plotting Layer Is Implemented
A future plotting-layer pass may add reusable plot-data builders and optional ggplot/autoplot outputs. Until that happens, the stable public contract is the current S3 plot() interface and its base-graphics output.

title: 7  Reporting And Inference
text:
7.1 summary()
This chapter centralizes reporting and inference labels so the estimator chapters can stay focused on workflows.
summary(fit_ols1)
summary(fit_kernel)
summary(fit_plr)
summary(fit_incremental)
summary() reports the scalar event and dynamic summaries stored by the fitted object. For scalar DML methods, read the DML inference label rather than assuming a bootstrap or refit procedure.

title: 7  Reporting And Inference
text:
7.2 fdid_contrast()


fdid_contrast(fit_kernel, g0 = eval_g[2], g1 = eval_g[7])
fdid_contrast(fit_flex, g0 = eval_g[2], g1 = eval_g[7],
              interpolate = TRUE)

fdid_contrast() reports a fixed-reference level contrast such as mu(g1) - mu(g0) for kernel or theta(g1) - theta(g0) for dml_flex.

title: 7  Reporting And Inference
text:
7.3 fdid_derivative()


fdid_derivative(fit_kernel, g0 = eval_g[5])
fdid_derivative(fit_flex, g0 = eval_g[5])

fdid_derivative() reports a derivative value at a fixed G. It is distinct from the scalar observed-population average derivative reported by dml_incremental.

title: 7  Reporting And Inference
section: 7.4 When Contrast SEs Use Stored Covariance
text:
7.4 When Contrast SEs Use Stored Covariance
Exact-grid contrasts can use stored covariance matrices when the fit provides them. Kernel bootstrap fits may store curve covariance matrices. dml_flex with signal_map = "blp_spline" can store finite-grid covariance matrices for level and derivative curves.

title: 7  Reporting And Inference
section: 7.5 When Contrast SEs Use Replicate Curves
text:
7.5 When Contrast SEs Use Replicate Curves
If stored replicate curves are available, contrast and value reporting can use the empirical replicate distribution. Kernel bootstrap fits and DML multiplier fits may provide these replicate arrays depending on options.

title: 7  Reporting And Inference
text:
7.6 When Intervals Are Pointwise Fallbacks
When covariance or replicate information is unavailable, reporting helpers may fall back to pointwise endpoint information. Label these as pointwise or approximate fallback intervals; do not present them as efficient contrast inference.

title: 7  Reporting And Inference
text:
7.7 How To Interpret Simultaneous Bands
Simultaneous bands are finite-grid statements over the stored eval_g grid. Kernel bootstrap bands are quantile-envelope bands. Non-BLP dml_flex bands are practical signal-mapping multiplier bands. BLP-spline bands use finite-grid covariance/Gaussian max-t calculations when available.

title: 7  Reporting And Inference
section: 7.8 What Is Bootstrap, What Is Analytical, What Is Multiplier
text:
7.8 What Is Bootstrap, What Is Analytical, What Is Multiplier






Label
Meaning



Analytical
Standard errors computed from fitted analytical formulas


Bootstrap
Stored resampled curve replicates or percentile intervals


Multiplier
Multiplier draws over stored influence or signal values


Gaussian max-t

Finite-grid critical value from a covariance matrix



The label should come from the fitted object whenever possible.

title: 7  Reporting And Inference
text:
7.9 Known Open Research-Level Inference Items
The package provides practical reporting for curves, contrasts, and derivatives. Research-level work remains for theorem-level efficient uniform DML bands and full influence-function storage for all non-BLP flexible curve paths. Until that changes, use conservative labels in reports.

title: 8  Sensitivity Analysis
8  Sensitivity Analysis
text:
8.2 Kernel Bandwidth And Support Sensitivity
Refit the kernel curve over plausible bandwidths and interior support windows. Report whether the substantive pattern changes when tails or mass points are excluded from the evaluation grid.

fit_kernel_h1 <- fdid(s_cont, tr_period, ref_period, method = "kernel",
                      eval_g = eval_g, h0 = 0.12)
fit_kernel_h2 <- fdid(s_cont, tr_period, ref_period, method = "kernel",
                      eval_g = eval_g, h0 = 0.24)

title: 8  Sensitivity Analysis
text:
8.3 Kernel Bootstrap Sensitivity
Use small bootstrap counts only for smoke checks. Increase bootstrap replications for reports and verify that pointwise intervals and quantile-envelope bands are stable enough for the claim being made.

title: 8  Sensitivity Analysis
text:
8.4 DML Learner Sensitivity
Compare transparent learners and flexible learners when optional packages are available. Keep the target fixed while varying learner.

fit_flex_linear <- fdid(s_cont, tr_period, ref_period, method = "dml_flex",
                        learner = "linear", eval_g = eval_g)
fit_flex_ridge <- fdid(s_cont, tr_period, ref_period, method = "dml_flex",
                       learner = "ridge", eval_g = eval_g)

title: 8  Sensitivity Analysis
text:
8.5 DML Density-Method Sensitivity
For dml_flex and dml_incremental, vary density_method because the conditional density enters the score. Large changes across density methods are diagnostic, especially for the incremental average derivative.

title: 8  Sensitivity Analysis
text:
8.6 Cross-Fitting And Repeated-Split Sensitivity
Vary K and S to check whether fold assignment and repeated-split aggregation drive the result. Report the values used in final tables.

title: 8  Sensitivity Analysis
text:
8.7 High-Dimensional Expansion Sensitivity
fdid_expand_covariates() can enrich the covariate design before DML estimation. Treat this as a design sensitivity check: more features can reduce misspecification but may increase variance and nuisance instability.

title: 8  Sensitivity Analysis
section: 8.8 How To Report Sensitivity Without Overclaiming
text:
8.8 How To Report Sensitivity Without Overclaiming
Report sensitivity by target. For example, say the kernel level curve is stable across bandwidths, or the incremental average derivative changes under different density methods. Avoid broad claims such as “all continuous-G methods agree” unless the compared objects truly estimate the same target.
